Using Pauses (Intonation in Non-Final Thought Groups)

A key strategy in being understood by others when you speak English is pausing between groups of words in your sentences. That means that you do not need to speak continuously - you pause for a very brief time between groups of words.
There are two reasons that you should pause when speaking:
1. It gives the listener time to process your speech.
When you take a short pause between thoughts when you are speaking, you give the person who is listening time to consider what you have said.

For example:
Why would you take time off now and not when everybody else has a vacation?
Why would you take time off now // and not when everybody else // has a vacation?
The second sentence is easier to understand since there are very brief pauses between each thought group.
1. It allows you to emphasize one or more main words in a sentence.

Pausing also helps the listener understand what has been said. When you speak, you put emphasis on the final content word in a group. This final stressed content word is also said with  a higher pitch.

For example:
Why would you take time off now // and not when everybody else // has a vacation?

When you speak, you put emphasis on the final content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) in thought group (now, else, vacation).

Homographs are words with different pronunciation and meanings but the same spelling. When you need to know how to pronounce homographs, you need to understand the context of the word. Then you can figure out the meaning of the word, and therefore know how to say the word correctly.
Here is a list of homographs. Notice that the spelling is the same but the meaning and pronunciation are different.

bass – (bAss) type of fish OR (bays) low, deep voice
bow – (boe) type of knot OR (bauw) to incline
entrance – (entrins) the way in OR (entrans)to delight
evening – (evuh -ning) smoothing out OR (evening) after sunset
learned – (learnd) past tense of learn OR (learnid) knowledgeable
minute – (maynute) tiny OR (minute) unit of time
row – (roe) line/ propel a boat OR (rauw) argument
wound – (wownd) past tense of wind OR (woond) to injure

images.text:
Todd stepped off the airport bus in front of the entrance to the central train station in Milan. Entranced, he scanned the area. Italy! Everything was amazing! He had four hours. What could he do until it was time to board the 3:00 p.m. train to Florence? There wasn't enough time to roam the streets and it was a little too long to be waiting around in the train station.
It was Todd's first time in Europe and the first time he had ever left the U.S. Every minute some minute thing caught his eye. The buildings were only a few stories high and more elaborate, and the people looked and walked differently. Todd couldn't stop staring at the people.

Everyone looked so chic and posh like in novels and stories. Even the sounds were novel: the musical tone of the Italian language, the shouting, the honking as motorbikes zoomed in and out of traffic. Todd felt as if he were in another universe. What a change from home!
He got out his Student Guidebook to Italy to read what it had to say about Milan. The Stazione Centrale square, he read, is full of pickpockets. Be especially careful not to walk around reading your guidebook, so no one will suspect you are a tourist and easy prey.
Todd slowly gazed around. Everyone suddenly looked like a suspect to him.

He thought, “I'll close the guidebook and go to a cafe close by.” When Todd approached the cafe, he realized that getting food might be a little difficult since he didn't know any Italian.
The friendly vendor brought out a selection of panini on a tray and Todd chose one. When the vendor said 'Coffee?' Todd nodded, smiling. The waiter returned with an espresso that smelled heavenly. Todd handed him some euros. He had started to relax.
Todd noticed that there were a lot of other young people milling around the station. They were from everywhere it seemed by their accents. Todd was really amazed at how small the world, which he had thought was so big, really was.
